issues.description: Regex `HAS_TIME` complects unit recognition with value parsing as a fast-path guard.
issues.detail: The pre-check `/\dm?s/i` is a cheap probe, not a parser, but it now lives next to the real `valueParser` call and silently encodes what counts as a time-like token. The two concerns (is-this-worth-parsing vs. what-is-it) are separable; a named predicate like `mayContainTime(value)` would make the time semantics explicit rather than hidden behind an anonymous regex.

issues.description: Regex can match non-time substrings inside identifiers or URLs (e.g. `1ms-foo`, `url(a1s.png)`).
issues.detail: `/\dm?s/i` matches any digit followed by optional `m` and a literal `s` anywhere in the value. That is fine as a fast reject but means the guard is not actually a predicate over time tokens; it is a predicate over any string containing `<digit>s` or `<digit>ms`. Worth a one-line comment naming it as an over-approximation, so future readers do not mistake it for a validator.

review.summary: The change is small and correct in spirit: skip the expensive `valueParser` call when the declaration value cannot contain a time token. That is a legitimate fast-path and the values/identities/time model of the rule is unchanged. My only notes are about clarity: the regex is an over-approximation acting as a guard, and it would read better as a named predicate with a one-line comment about what it intentionally does not promise. SIMPLE enough; no decomposition required.
